direct_answer:
Shell states it conducted a double materiality assessment in 2024 as the basis for its ESRS Sustainability Statements, assessing (i) impact materiality (actual/potential impacts on people and the environment) and (ii) financial materiality (sustainability-related risks/opportunities that could reasonably be expected to trigger material financial effects) [Source 2]. The process follows five steps: establish business context (activities, value chain and stakeholders), identify potential sustainability matters and related impacts/risks/opportunities, assess impacts for severity (actual and potential) and assess risks/opportunities for potential financial effects, then determine material matters for reporting [Source 4].

For impact assessment, Shell rates magnitude for actual impacts after standard control measures and rates likelihood and magnitude for potential impacts; potential magnitude is assessed on a gross basis (assuming no mitigation from control measures), and for potential human rights impacts magnitude takes precedence over likelihood [Source 3]. For financial assessment, Shell applies likelihood and magnitude criteria based on its enterprise risk management framework (modified for consistency with impact assessment), using five-point scales and considering how financial effects could arise including via dependencies on natural, human and social resources [Source 3]. Shell then applies reporting thresholds (actual impacts: magnitude; potential impacts: likelihood+magnitude; risks: existing financial materiality definitions; opportunities: qualitative thresholds), with final results reviewed/endorsed by an internal management committee [Source 3]. Shell maps identified IROs to ESRS disclosure requirements; requirements with at least one corresponding IRO are deemed material [Source 7].

Stakeholder consideration: Shell says it engages stakeholders regularly on potential business impacts, but did not engage stakeholders directly on the double materiality assessment; instead it used feedback from existing communication channels and reviewed the assessment with relationship owners for key stakeholder groups [Source 6].

Outcomes: Shell reports the assessment identified 23 material impacts (16 negative, 7 positive) [Source 5]. It also states that greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are a material impact and that this corresponds to both a risk and an opportunity (i.e., material from both an impact and a financial perspective) [Source 5]. Shell further specifies that it identified “GHG emissions” as a material impact and “climate change and energy transition” as a sustainability-related risk [Source 12].

Other sustainability matters Shell explicitly says were identified as “material topics” by its double materiality assessment include: biodiversity loss, sensitive areas and species, and ecosystem services [Source 9]; waste management [Source 14]; culture of integrity and responsible sourcing (and entity-specific topics: tax and payments to governments, and safety) [Source 10]; and (for affected communities) social impacts, community engagement, security and human rights, and social investment and benefits [Source 15]. However, based on the retrieved passages, Shell does not explicitly state which of these are material from both impact and financial perspectives; it indicates that, aside from GHG emissions, “the remaining impacts do not constitute a risk or opportunity in their own right” [Source 5].
compliance_rationale: The passages provide a clear description of Shell’s double materiality process (steps, criteria, thresholds, governance review) and explain how stakeholders’ views were considered (via existing channels, not direct engagement for the assessment) [Sources 3, 4, 6, 7]. The outcomes are partially evidenced: Shell discloses that GHG emissions are both a material impact and linked to a material risk/opportunity, satisfying identification of at least one matter material in both dimensions [Sources 5, 12]. But the retrieved evidence does not include the referenced “Material sustainability topics” table (pp. 352-353) that would be needed to list all matters material from both impact and financial perspectives; Shell also indicates most other impacts are not risks/opportunities in their own right [Source 5].
disclosure_gaps: The full list/table of material sustainability topics (referenced as being on pp. 352-353) is not included in the retrieved passages, limiting identification of all matters that are material from both impact and financial perspectives [Source 5].
Explicit identification, for each material topic, of whether it is impact material, financially material, or both is not provided in the retrieved passages (except for GHG emissions) [Sources 5, 12].

More detail on the specific qualitative/quantitative thresholds (numerical cut-offs) used to determine materiality is not provided in the retrieved passages (only that thresholds are used and the general basis for thresholds) [Sources 1, 3, 5].
key_findings: Shell performed an ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment in 2024, considering both impact materiality and financial materiality [Source 2].
Shell’s process follows five steps: business context/value chain/stakeholders; identify matters and IROs; assess impacts and financial effects; determine material matters for reporting [Source 4].

Impact assessment uses magnitude/likelihood ratings; potential impacts are assessed gross (no mitigation), and for potential human rights impacts magnitude takes precedence over likelihood [Source 3].
Financial assessment uses likelihood and magnitude criteria (five-point scales) based on enterprise risk management and considers dependencies on natural, human and social resources [Source 3].

Stakeholders were not engaged directly on the double materiality assessment; Shell used feedback from existing channels and reviewed the assessment with relationship owners for key stakeholder groups [Source 6].
Shell identified 23 material impacts (16 negative, 7 positive) [Source 5].

GHG emissions are identified as a material impact and also correspond to both a risk and an opportunity; Shell also identifies climate change and the energy transition as a sustainability-related risk [Sources 5, 12].

Shell identifies additional material topics including biodiversity loss/sensitive areas and species/ecosystem services; waste management; culture of integrity/responsible sourcing (plus entity-specific: tax and payments to governments; safety); and affected-community topics (social impacts, community engagement, security and human rights, social investment and benefits) [Sources 9, 10, 14, 15].
